claim: De novo mutations underlie individually rare but collectively common pediatric congenital disorders.
source: De novo mutations underlie individually rare but collectively common pediatric congenital disorders.
evidence: This is a general statement about the role of de novo mutations in pediatric disorders, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Some de novo mutations can be detected in tissues and from cells in a parent, where their abundance and tissue distribution can be measured.
source: Some of these mutations can also be detected in tissues and from cells in a parent, where their abundance and tissue distribution can be measured.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior research and is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: A subset of de novo mutations is detectable in sperm from the father and predicted to impact the health of offspring.
source: We previously reported that a subset of these mutations is detectable in sperm from the father, predicted to impact the health of offspring.
evidence: This claim references the authors' previous work and is supported by citation to their prior research.

claim: Three independent couples undergoing in vitro fertilization were recruited for the study.
source: As a cohort study, in three independent couples undergoing in vitro fertilization, we first identified male gonadal mosaicism through deep whole genome sequencing.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design and participant recruitment.

claim: Male gonadal mosaicism was identified through deep whole genome sequencing.
source: As a cohort study, in three independent couples undergoing in vitro fertilization, we first identified male gonadal mosaicism through deep whole genome sequencing.
evidence: This describes the methodology used to identify gonadal mosaicism in the study.

claim: Variants were confirmed and their transmission to preimplantation blastocysts (32 total) was assessed through targeted ultra-deep genotyping.
source: We then confirmed variants and assessed their transmission to preimplantation blastocysts (32 total) through targeted ultra-deep genotyping.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and sample size used in the study.

claim: Across 55 gonadal mosaic variants, 15 were transmitted to blastocysts for a total of 19 transmission events.
source: Across 55 gonadal mosaic variants, 15 were transmitted to blastocysts for a total of 19 transmission events.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results from the study.

claim: The transmission represented an overall predictable but slight undertransmission based upon the measured mutational abundance in sperm.
source: This represented an overall predictable but slight undertransmission based upon the measured mutational abundance in sperm.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data comparing observed to expected transmission rates.

claim: The conclusion of predictable transmission and slight undertransmission was replicated in an independent, previously published family-based cohort.
source: We replicated this conclusion in an independent, previously published family-based cohort.
evidence: This describes replication analysis using previously published data.

claim: Unbiased preimplantation genetic testing for gonadal mosaicism may represent a feasible approach to reduce the transmission of potentially harmful de novo mutations.
source: Unbiased preimplantation genetic testing for gonadal mosaicism may represent a feasible approach to reduce the transmission of potentially harmful de novo mutations.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study findings about the potential clinical application.

claim: Preimplantation genetic testing for gonadal mosaicism could help to reduce the impact of de novo mutations on miscarriages and pediatric disease.
source: This—in turn—could help to reduce their impact on miscarriages and pediatric disease.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical benefits based on the study findings.

claim: Mosaic mutations are commonly recognized in cancers or localized overgrowth disorders, such as Proteus, CLOVES, and hemimegalencephaly syndromes.
source: Mosaic mutations are commonly recognized in cancers or localized overgrowth disorders, such as Proteus, CLOVES, and hemimegalencephaly syndromes (Lee et al., 2012; Lindhurst et al., 2011; Goncalves et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on mosaic mutations in various disorders.

claim: Mosaic mutations are increasingly recognized in more complex diseases such as autism spectrum disorder or structural abnormalities.
source: Increasingly recognized in more complex diseases such as autism spectrum disorder or structural abnormalities (Jamuar et al., 2014; Rodin et al., 2021,) mosaic mutations are typically restricted to the individual in which they arise unless they appear prior to the embryonic separation of somatic and germline lineages or within germ cell progenitors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to research on mosaic mutations in complex diseases.

claim: Mosaic mutations are typically restricted to the individual in which they arise unless they appear prior to the embryonic separation of somatic and germline lineages or within germ cell progenitors.
source: Increasingly recognized in more complex diseases such as autism spectrum disorder or structural abnormalities (Jamuar et al., 2014; Rodin et al., 2021,) mosaic mutations are typically restricted to the individual in which they arise unless they appear prior to the embryonic separation of somatic and germline lineages or within germ cell progenitors.
evidence: This describes the biological basis for when mosaic mutations can be transmitted, based on established developmental biology knowledge.

claim: Gonadal mosaic mutations have the potential to transmit to offspring.
source: In these cases, gonadal mosaic mutations (comprising gonad specific and gonosomal) have the potential to transmit to offspring.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the timing of mutation occurrence relative to germline development.

claim: Gonadal mosaic mutations may result in miscarriage or a congenital or complex disease—often without phenotypes in the parents.
source: These will appear as a considerable portion of de novo mutations and may result in miscarriage or a congenital or complex disease—often without phenotypes in the parents (Breuss et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on the consequences of gonadal mosaic mutations.

claim: 5–20% of identified pathogenic de novo mutations in a child are detectable in parental tissues.
source: We and others previously demonstrated that 5–20% of identified pathogenic de novo mutations in a child are detectable in parental tissues, with ejaculated sperm demonstrating the highest rate of occurrence (Yang et al., 2020; Breuss et al., 2020; Myers et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple prior studies quantifying parental mosaicism.

claim: Ejaculated sperm demonstrates the highest rate of occurrence of detectable pathogenic de novo mutations among parental tissues.
source: We and others previously demonstrated that 5–20% of identified pathogenic de novo mutations in a child are detectable in parental tissues, with ejaculated sperm demonstrating the highest rate of occurrence (Yang et al., 2020; Breuss et al., 2020; Myers et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research comparing mutation detection rates across tissues.

claim: Every male harbors up to dozens of gonadal mosaic mutations in sperm.
source: Every male harbors up to dozens of such mutations in sperm, which—in contrast to other paternal mutation types that increase with age (Jónsson et al., 2017)—contribute a life-long threat of transmission largely independent of paternal age (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research quantifying gonadal mosaic mutations in males.

claim: Gonadal mosaic mutations contribute a life-long threat of transmission largely independent of paternal age.
source: Every male harbors up to dozens of such mutations in sperm, which—in contrast to other paternal mutation types that increase with age (Jónsson et al., 2017)—contribute a life-long threat of transmission largely independent of paternal age (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research on the age-independence of gonadal mosaic mutations.

claim: Other paternal mutation types increase with age.
source: Every male harbors up to dozens of such mutations in sperm, which—in contrast to other paternal mutation types that increase with age (Jónsson et al., 2017)—contribute a life-long threat of transmission largely independent of paternal age (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research on age-related paternal mutations.

claim: Gonadal mosaic mutations are thought to explain, in part, the individually rare but collectively common risk of congenital disorders from de novo mutations.
source: As such, they are thought to explain, in part, the individually rare but collectively common risk of congenital disorders from de novo mutations (Deciphering Developmental Disorders, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research on the contribution of de novo mutations to congenital disorders.

claim: Experimental evidence of transmission to a conceptus of in situ identified gonadal mosaic mutations is lacking.
source: Yet, experimental evidence of transmission to a conceptus of in situ identified gonadal mosaic mutations—in contrast to the detection of gonadal mosaicism of already transmitted variants—is lacking.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the existing literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Procedures like preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) could be used to select embryos absent for potentially damaging mutations detected in sperm.
source: This is a critical point upon which clinical implementation hinges because procedures like preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) could be used to select embryos absent for potentially damaging mutations detected in sperm.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical applications based on the study's premise.

claim: Gonadal mosaic mutations detected in sperm from individual males can transmit to their preimplantation blastocysts.
source: Here, we demonstrate that gonadal mosaic mutations detected in sperm from individual males can transmit to their preimplantation blastocysts.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The study assessed transmission at the preimplantation blastocyst stage to avoid potential bias introduced by selection of mosaic mutations or their lineages during implantation or survival.
source: We decided to assess this early time point, as it avoids any potential bias introduced by a possible selection of mosaic mutations or their lineages during implantation or survival.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the study design choice based on methodological considerations.

claim: Three infertile couples (F01, F02, and F03) who had supernumerary blastocysts (minimum of 8) were recruited for gonadal mosaicism assessment.
source: For gonadal mosaicism assessment, we recruited three infertile couples (F01, F02, and F03) who had supernumerary blastocysts (minimum of 8) that wanted to donate them to research.
evidence: This describes the study population and recruitment criteria.

claim: The males provided a fresh ejaculate and a somatic sample (blood for F01, saliva for F02 and F03).
source: The males ('sperm donors') all provided a fresh ejaculate and a somatic sample (blood for F01, saliva for F02 and F03).
evidence: This describes the sample collection from study participants.

claim: The age of the three sperm donors was 36, 38, and 50 years for F01, F02, and F03, respectively.
source: The age of the three sperm donors was 36, 38, and 50 years for F01, F02, and F03, respectively.
evidence: This provides demographic information about the study participants.

claim: The three fathers' ancestries were most closely matched to Middle Eastern (F01) or European (F02 and F03) ancestry.
source: In accordance with reported population origin, the three fathers' ancestries were most closely matched to Middle Eastern (F01) or European (F02 and F03) ancestry, employing nearest neighbor analysis of principle components (Taliun et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the genetic ancestry analysis of the study participants.

claim: Whole-genome sequencing of the sperm donor samples was performed to approximately 300× read depth.
source: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS; NovaSeq 6000, Illumina) of the sperm donor samples was performed to approximately 300× (Supplementary file 1) as described (Yang et al., 2021), then analyzed using the 300× MSMF (MuTect2, Strelka2, MosaicForecast) computational pipeline (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the sequencing methodology used in the study.

claim: The 300× MSMF computational pipeline demonstrates a 90% specificity and sensitivity of >95% for mutations at allelic fractions above 0.03.
source: This pipeline demonstrates a 90% specificity and sensitivity of >95% for mutations at allelic fractions (AFs) above 0.03 (Ref Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the performance characteristics of the computational pipeline, supported by citation.

claim: The false-negative rate for transmission detection in whole-genome-amplified blastocyst material is approximately 0.06.
source: We found that transmission followed expected genetic patterns; furthermore, homozygous variants from a parent—which should be present across all blastocysts—were transmitted in approximately 94% of those analyzed, suggesting a false-negative rate of ~0.06.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data on transmission of homozygous variants.

claim: The false-positive rate for MPAS detection of gonadal mosaic mutations in blastocysts is approximately 0.001.
source: Conversely, when assessing the presence of gonadal mosaic mutations identified in one sperm donor in the blastocysts of the other two, we only found one such event out of 985 possible, suggesting an MPAS false-positive rate of ~0.001.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data on cross-contamination or false-positive detection.

claim: Whole-genome-amplified blastocysts exhibit modest allelic dropout.
source: Thus, this approach provides sensitivity to detect clinically relevant gonadal mosaicism (i.e., mutations with a measurable and potentially actionably abundance) and specificity to assess transmissions of perm mosaic mutations to blastocysts, and it suggests that whole-genome-amplified blastocysts exhibit modest allelic dropout, even though allelic imbalance was frequently observed.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed false-negative rate and transmission patterns.

claim: The three sperm donors harbored a combined 55 detected gonadal mosaic mutations.
source: The three sperm donors harbored a combined 55 detected gonadal mosaic mutations—mostly single-nucleotide mutations—with the potential to be transmitted to offspring (F01: 12, F02: 13, and F03: 30) (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results, with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: F01 harbored 12 gonadal mosaic mutations, F02 harbored 13, and F03 harbored 30.
source: The three sperm donors harbored a combined 55 detected gonadal mosaic mutations—mostly single-nucleotide mutations—with the potential to be transmitted to offspring (F01: 12, F02: 13, and F03: 30) (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This provides the breakdown of mutations per individual, supported by figure references.

claim: The difference in mutation number between F01/F02 and F03 likely represents expected biological variability within the previously observed range.
source: While F01 and F02 differed by more than twofold from F03, this likely represents expected biological variability that is within the previously observed range (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed variation, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: None of the variants were predicted to impair health when heterozygous.
source: None of the variants were predicted to impair health when heterozygous, and they, thus, serve as likely neutral variants to model transmission.
evidence: This describes the predicted functional impact of the identified variants.

claim: The gonadal mosaic mutations were present at allelic fractions between 0.003 and 0.247 (mean: 0.047; standard deviation: 0.055).
source: These mutations were present at AFs between 0.003 and 0.247 (mean: 0.047; standard deviation: 0.055), with those of lower AF typically restricted to sperm ('Sperm') and those of higher AF typically found in both sperm and blood or saliva ('Shared') (Figure 1c, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This provides quantitative data on the allelic fractions of detected mutations.

claim: Mutations of lower allelic fraction are typically restricted to sperm ('Sperm').
source: These mutations were present at AFs between 0.003 and 0.247 (mean: 0.047; standard deviation: 0.055), with those of lower AF typically restricted to sperm ('Sperm') and those of higher AF typically found in both sperm and blood or saliva ('Shared') (Figure 1c, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the tissue distribution pattern of mutations based on their allelic fraction.

claim: Mutations of higher allelic fraction are typically found in both sperm and blood or saliva ('Shared').
source: These mutations were present at AFs between 0.003 and 0.247 (mean: 0.047; standard deviation: 0.055), with those of lower AF typically restricted to sperm ('Sperm') and those of higher AF typically found in both sperm and blood or saliva ('Shared') (Figure 1c, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the tissue distribution pattern of mutations based on their allelic fraction.

claim: The number, distribution, and abundance of detected mutations were consistent with other unbiased analyses performed previously.
source: Overall, their number, distribution, and abundance were consistent with other unbiased analyses performed previously (Breuss et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This compares the current findings to prior published work, supported by citations.

claim: The sperm donor F01 (36 years of age) had an excessive number of soma-specific mutations at lower allelic fractions, evidencing early clonal hematopoiesis.
source: Of note, similar to our prior observations (Yang et al., 2021), the sperm donor F01 (36 years of age) had an excessive number of soma-specific mutations ('Soma') at lower AFs, evidencing early clonal hematopoiesis (Breuss et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed mutation pattern, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: For F02, two of the eight blastocysts did not show overall high quality in the MPAS for gonadal mosaic variants and were excluded from subsequent analyses.
source: For F02, two of the eight blastocysts did not show overall high quality in the MPAS for gonadal mosaic variants and thus were excluded from subsequent analyses.
evidence: This describes quality control measures applied to the data.

claim: Mutations of higher allelic fraction evidenced higher blastocyst transmission rates than those of lower allelic fraction.
source: Consistent with a model where the risk of transmission is proportional to sperm AF, mutations of higher AF evidenced higher blastocyst transmission rates than those of lower AF (R = 0.67, p value = 2.9e−8, Pearson correlation, Methods).
evidence: This describes a correlation observed in the data with statistical support.

claim: The risk of transmission is proportional to sperm allelic fraction.
source: Consistent with a model where the risk of transmission is proportional to sperm AF, mutations of higher AF evidenced higher blastocyst transmission rates than those of lower AF (R = 0.67, p value = 2.9e−8, Pearson correlation, Methods).
evidence: This is a model supported by the observed correlation between AF and transmission rate.

claim: Cosegregation of mutations of almost equal allelic fraction was observed.
source: Although additional mutations may arise within earlier sperm lineages marked by prior mutations (e.g., blastocyst #2 in F03), somewhat unexpectedly, we observed cosegregation of mutations of almost equal AF (e.g., blastocyst #1 in F02 or blastocyst #6 in F03); this was reflected as a nonrandom distribution of transmitted mutations across blastocysts in F03 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes an unexpected pattern observed in the transmission data.

claim: A nonrandom distribution of transmitted mutations across blastocysts was observed in F03.
source: Although additional mutations may arise within earlier sperm lineages marked by prior mutations (e.g., blastocyst #2 in F03), somewhat unexpectedly, we observed cosegregation of mutations of almost equal AF (e.g., blastocyst #1 in F02 or blastocyst #6 in F03); this was reflected as a nonrandom distribution of transmitted mutations across blastocysts in F03 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes a statistical pattern in the transmission data, with reference to supporting figure.

claim: Some early male germ cell lineages or individual mitotic divisions are more susceptible to mutation than others.
source: This suggests that some early male germ cell lineages or individual mitotic divisions are more susceptible to mutation than others, allowing stratification of sperm lineages into those with higher and those with lower mosaic load, and mutations from one sperm progenitor may uncouple during meiosis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed cosegregation and nonrandom distribution patterns.

claim: Mutations from one sperm progenitor may uncouple during meiosis.
source: This suggests that some early male germ cell lineages or individual mitotic divisions are more susceptible to mutation than others, allowing stratification of sperm lineages into those with higher and those with lower mosaic load, and mutations from one sperm progenitor may uncouple during meiosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of different combinations of mutations across blastocysts.

claim: Different combinations of gonadal mosaic mutations were observed across blastocysts.
source: Indeed, we observed different combinations of gonadal mosaic mutations across blastocysts (e.g., blastocysts #5, #6, and #9 in F03).
evidence: This describes a pattern observed in the transmission data.

claim: For both F01 and F02, the observed transmission rate was within the 95% confidence interval of the expectation.
source: Whereas for both F01 and F02 the observed transmission rate was within the 95% confidence interval of the expectation, for F03 and across all individuals when considered in total, the transmission was slightly below what was expected (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This compares observed to expected transmission rates with statistical measures.

claim: For F03 and across all individuals when considered in total, the transmission was slightly below what was expected.
source: Whereas for both F01 and F02 the observed transmission rate was within the 95% confidence interval of the expectation, for F03 and across all individuals when considered in total, the transmission was slightly below what was expected (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This compares observed to expected transmission rates with statistical measures.

claim: The undertransmission likely reflects a limitation of the model which assumes that gonadal mosaic mutations arise and transmit independently.
source: This likely reflects a limitation of the model which assumes that gonadal mosaic mutations arise and transmit independently—a simplification, as mutations arising on the same lineage have the potential to cotransmit.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed undertransmission based on model assumptions.

claim: Mutations arising on the same lineage have the potential to cotransmit.
source: This likely reflects a limitation of the model which assumes that gonadal mosaic mutations arise and transmit independently—a simplification, as mutations arising on the same lineage have the potential to cotransmit.
evidence: This is a biological inference about mutation transmission based on lineage relationships.

claim: The undertransmission may be especially relevant if sperm lineages do not stochastically accumulate mutations during early development.
source: This may be especially relevant if sperm lineages do not stochastically accumulate mutations during early development.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed undertransmission pattern.

claim: The observations closely reflect expectations, suggesting that gonadal mosaicism assessment can serve as a predictor of mutation transmission.
source: Nevertheless, our observations closely reflect expectations, suggesting that gonadal mosaicism assessment can serve as a predictor of mutation transmission.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of observed and expected transmission rates.

claim: The 55 gonadal mosaic mutations were distributed across all chromosomes except for chromosomes 19, 22, and X/Y.
source: The 55 gonadal mosaic mutations were distributed across all chromosomes—except for chromosomes 19, 22, and X/Y—roughly as expected based on chromosomal length.
evidence: This describes the chromosomal distribution of detected mutations.

claim: The chromosomal distribution of mutations was roughly as expected based on chromosomal length.
source: The 55 gonadal mosaic mutations were distributed across all chromosomes—except for chromosomes 19, 22, and X/Y—roughly as expected based on chromosomal length.
evidence: This compares the observed distribution to expectations based on chromosome size.

claim: The vast majority of mutations was found in intergenic (n = 28) or intronic (n = 24) regions.
source: As expected based on prior work, the vast majority was found in intergenic (n = 28) or intronic (n = 24) regions; one mutation each was found in a 5′-UTR, the intron of a noncoding RNA, and an exon.
evidence: This describes the genomic location distribution of detected mutations.

claim: One mutation was found in a 5′-UTR, one in the intron of a noncoding RNA, and one in an exon.
source: As expected based on prior work, the vast majority was found in intergenic (n = 28) or intronic (n = 24) regions; one mutation each was found in a 5′-UTR, the intron of a noncoding RNA, and an exon.
evidence: This describes the genomic location of specific mutations.

claim: The exonic mutation (F03, AF = 0.063) resulted in a nonsynonymous SNV in RABGAP1 (NM_012197; p.Asp74Gly).
source: The exonic mutation (F03, AF = 0.063) resulted in a nonsynonymous SNV in RABGAP1 (NM_012197; p.Asp74Gly), a rare, previously reported mutation (allele frequency of 7.96e−6) with no known disease association.
evidence: This describes the specific characteristics of the one exonic mutation detected.

claim: The RABGAP1 mutation is a rare, previously reported mutation (allele frequency of 7.96e−6) with no known disease association.
source: The exonic mutation (F03, AF = 0.063) resulted in a nonsynonymous SNV in RABGAP1 (NM_012197; p.Asp74Gly), a rare, previously reported mutation (allele frequency of 7.96e−6) with no known disease association.
evidence: This provides information about the frequency and clinical significance of the mutation.

claim: Reanalysis of the REACH cohort was performed by combining the list of detected gonadal mosaic mutations with previously established variants called from trio WGS.
source: Reanalysis of the REACH cohort data was performed by combining the list of detected gonadal mosaic mutation (Breuss et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021) with previously established variants called from the trio WGS (Brandler et al., 2018; Brandler et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the methodology for the replication analysis using previously published data.

claim: In the REACH cohort, across 131 sperm-detectable mosaic variants, nine transmissions among seven unique variants were observed.
source: Across 131 sperm-detectable mosaic variants, we observed nine transmissions among seven unique variants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This reports the results of the replication analysis in the REACH cohort.

claim: In the REACH cohort, the observed transmission rate was slightly below the expected 95% confidence interval when combining analysis of the eight families.
source: As this cohort had a lower number of observable transmission events per paternal sample due to the lower number of fertilization events (1–3 offspring compared to 8–14 blastocysts) and lower sequencing depth, we combined analysis of the eight families. The observed transmission rate was again slightly below the expected 95% confidence interval (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b, c).
evidence: This reports the statistical comparison of observed to expected transmission in the REACH cohort.

claim: The replication in live-born offspring supports the undertransmission observed in blastocysts.
source: This replication in live-born offspring supports the undertransmission observed in blastocysts and highlights the potential predictive power of gonadal mosaicism assessment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the consistency between the blastocyst and live-born offspring results.

claim: The replication in live-born offspring highlights the potential predictive power of gonadal mosaicism assessment.
source: This replication in live-born offspring supports the undertransmission observed in blastocysts and highlights the potential predictive power of gonadal mosaicism assessment.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the clinical implications based on the replication results.

claim: The study directly measured the abundance of gonadal mosaic variants and demonstrated transmission to preimplantation blastocysts for three couples undergoing IVF.
source: Here, we directly measured the abundance of gonadal mosaic variants and demonstrate transmission to preimplantation blastocysts for three couples undergoing IVF.
evidence: This summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: The results provide proof-of-concept that a priori detected gonadal mosaic mutations can transmit to blastocysts and therefore likely to offspring.
source: These results provide a proof-of-concept that a priori detected gonadal mosaic mutations can transmit to blastocysts and therefore likely to offspring.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the study findings.

claim: The study was only able to ascertain the phenomenon in three sperm donors and their associated blastocysts.
source: There are two important limitations of our study: (1) we were only able to ascertain this phenomenon in three sperm donors and their associated blastocysts; (2) none of the variants interrogated for this study were predicted to be disease causing.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study regarding sample size.

claim: None of the variants interrogated for this study were predicted to be disease causing.
source: There are two important limitations of our study: (1) we were only able to ascertain this phenomenon in three sperm donors and their associated blastocysts; (2) none of the variants interrogated for this study were predicted to be disease causing.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation regarding the clinical relevance of the specific variants studied.

claim: If this approach is to be advanced in the clinic to prevent genetic disease, further research is necessary that expands the size of the cohort and directly assesses a priori identified pathogenic variants for transmission to blastocysts.
source: Thus, if this approach is to be advanced in the clinic to prevent genetic disease, further research is necessary that expands the size of the cohort and directly assesses a priori identified pathogenic variants for transmission to blastocysts.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the study limitations.

claim: Further technological development will be required to enable the direct assessment of mutations from biopsies rather than whole blastocysts.
source: In addition, further technological development will be required to enable the direct assessment of mutations from biopsies rather than whole blastocysts as implemented in this study.
evidence: This identifies a technical limitation and need for future development.

claim: Previous studies focused on the detection of mosaicism in parents following the identification of de novo mutations in offspring.
source: Previous studies focused on the detection of mosaicism in parents following the identification of de novo mutations in offspring (Breuss et al., 2020; Rahbari et al., 2016; Jónsson et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the approach of prior research, supported by citations.

claim: Following the birth of a child with a disease due to a de novo mutation, parents are provided with an empirical recurrence risk of 1–2% for future pregnancies.
source: Currently, following the birth of a child with a disease due to a de novo mutation, parents are provided with an empirical recurrence risk of 1–2% for future pregnancies.
evidence: This describes current clinical practice for genetic counseling.

claim: The population recurrence risk of 1-2% reflects an average of a near-zero risk in the majority and measurably higher risk (up to 25%) in a minority of instances due to gonadal mosaicism.
source: However, this population risk reflects an average of a near-zero risk in the majority and measurably higher risk (up to 25%) in a minority of instances due to gonadal mosaicism (Campbell et al., 2014).
evidence: This explains the heterogeneity underlying population-level recurrence risk estimates, supported by citation.

claim: Recent studies have improved the risk accuracy by incorporating population models and sampling parental blood.
source: While recent studies have improved the risk accuracy by incorporating population models and sampling parental blood (Jónsson et al., 2018; Campbell et al., 2014), direct assessment of gonadal mosaicism can provide a more precise personalized risk, as well as the potential to prevent recurrence through genetic testing.
evidence: This describes advances in risk assessment methods, supported by citations.

claim: Direct assessment of gonadal mosaicism can provide a more precise personalized risk and the potential to prevent recurrence through genetic testing.
source: While recent studies have improved the risk accuracy by incorporating population models and sampling parental blood (Jónsson et al., 2018; Campbell et al., 2014), direct assessment of gonadal mosaicism can provide a more precise personalized risk, as well as the potential to prevent recurrence through genetic testing.
evidence: This is a claim about the potential advantages of the approach described in the study.

claim: The framework of detecting mosaicism after a child is born is only applicable to families where a de novo mutation has previously been identified.
source: Yet, this framework is only applicable to families where a de novo mutations has previously been identified, and it can merely prevent recurrence within a family.
evidence: This identifies a limitation of the reactive approach to gonadal mosaicism detection.

claim: The reactive framework can merely prevent recurrence within a family.
source: Yet, this framework is only applicable to families where a de novo mutations has previously been identified, and it can merely prevent recurrence within a family.
evidence: This identifies a limitation of the reactive approach to gonadal mosaicism detection.

claim: The authors previously demonstrated their ability to detect gonadal mosaicism in males independent of prior transmission.
source: While we previously demonstrated our ability to detect gonadal mosaicism in males independent of prior transmission (Breuss et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021), this study provides the important complement that these detected variants are, indeed, transmitted to the next generation.
evidence: This references prior work by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: This study provides the important complement that detected variants are transmitted to the next generation.
source: While we previously demonstrated our ability to detect gonadal mosaicism in males independent of prior transmission (Breuss et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021), this study provides the important complement that these detected variants are, indeed, transmitted to the next generation.
evidence: This describes the novel contribution of the current study.

claim: 1 in 15 males carry a potentially pathogenic mutation, detectable in approximately 5% of sperm cells.
source: We previously estimated that 1 in 15 males carry a potentially pathogenic mutation, detectable in approximately 5% of sperm cells (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: A gonadal mosaic variant may result in adverse pregnancy or pediatric health outcomes for 1 in 300 concepti.
source: Together, this led to a prediction that a gonadal mosaic variant may result in adverse pregnancy or pediatric health outcomes for 1 in 300 concepti (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a prediction based on prior estimates, supported by citation.

claim: Gonadal mosaic variants likely represent approximately 15% of the monogenic sporadic component of diseases such as autism or congenital heart disease.
source: While this likely only represents ~15% of the monogenic sporadic component of diseases such as autism or congenital heart disease, this is the sole fraction that could be prevented with further advances.
evidence: This is an estimate of the proportion of disease attributable to gonadal mosaicism.

claim: Gonadal mosaic variants represent the sole fraction of monogenic sporadic disease that could be prevented with further advances.
source: While this likely only represents ~15% of the monogenic sporadic component of diseases such as autism or congenital heart disease, this is the sole fraction that could be prevented with further advances.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the preventability of different types of de novo mutations.
